title: 20 Years In
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: On the eve of his 20th year of teaching high school in Cedar Springs, Michigan, Dave Stuart Jr. reflects on the specific people who shaped him as a teacher rather than framing the milestone as a personal achievement. He names a high school computer science teacher he's now nervous to emulate while teaching AP Computer Science Principles himself, his mother's essay feedback, mentor and author Jim Burke, Malcolm X's autobiography, his current colleagues, and his grandfather's counterintuitive lesson in wise laziness. His central argument is that even after two decades, facing a new class of 153 students still feels daunting, and that the confidence to do it doesn't come from solo self-reliance but from consciously remembering the 'massive conspiracy of people' whose influence continues to prop up his teaching.
points: Stuart frames 20 years of teaching not as personal mastery but as the accumulated influence of specific people, naming a former teacher, his mother, mentor Jim Burke, Malcolm X's autobiography, colleagues, and his grandfather by name.

He is candid that even 20 years in, facing a new roster still produces genuine self-doubt: 'Twenty years in, heading into a school year still feels daunting. It's that whole, "Wait, do I actually know how to do this?" thing.'

His closing reframe rejects the self-made-teacher narrative outright: 'If it were all up to me — just Dave Stuart, all by himself — I'd be doomed... it's not. The teacher my students will meet tomorrow is in fact propped up by a massive conspiracy of people.'

The personal detail of teaching AP Computer Science Principles this year, a subject his own high school computer science teacher first introduced him to, illustrates how directly past mentors shape a teacher's ongoing curriculum choices decades later.
quotes: Tomorrow begins the 20th year of my teaching career, and as of this moment's rosters (sure to change still) I've got 153 human beings that I'll be getting to know in the weeks to come.
I think of Malcolm X, whose autobiography shifted something inside of me over twenty years ago in my college dormitory as I witnessed how an education transformed a mind and thereby a life.
I think of my mom, who gave me feedback on my high school English essays before I turned them in, and what a privilege it is to get to do some of that for students each year.
Twenty years in, heading into a school year still feels daunting. It's that whole, "Wait, do I actually know how to do this?" thing.
But: it's not. The teacher my students will meet tomorrow is in fact propped up by a massive conspiracy of people who have worked together to make me the guy for the job.
I think of my grandfather, who taught me to be lazy in a manner befitting wisdom.
